sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0, defined in 2014, that standardizes how a client obtains authenticated user identity by issuing a signed ID Token (a JWT) alongside the access token, plus a standardized `/userinfo` endpoint for retrieving claims.

OAuth 2.0 was designed to solve delegated authorization — "let this app access my calendar" — not authentication. But by 2012, almost every implementation of OAuth was being used for login: "log in with Google," "log in with Facebook," "log in with Microsoft." The problem was that OAuth 2.0 had no standardized way to communicate who the user actually was. The access token is opaque to the client (and should be — the client does not need to read it), the resource server's API (Google's `/userinfo` or Facebook's `/me`) is non-standard, and the user's identity is implicit rather than explicit. This produced a decade of confused implementations: developers inspected access tokens they should not have parsed, trusted unverified `user_id` parameters in redirect URLs, and hit non-standard per-provider APIs to fetch the user's email. OpenID Connect (OIDC), published in 2014, fixed this by adding a standardized identity layer: every successful OIDC authentication returns an ID Token — a JWT signed by the provider — that explicitly states who the user is, when they authenticated, and to whom the token was issued. By 2024, Google Sign-In, Microsoft Accounts, Apple Sign In, Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, and Azure AD all speak OIDC, and "Log in with X" almost always means OIDC under the hood.

The key innovation is the ID Token. Unlike an OAuth 2.0 access token, which is intended for the resource server, the ID Token is intended for the client — it is the proof that the user authenticated, addressed to the client, and signed by the provider. The ID Token is a JWT (see Topic 3) with standardized claims: `iss` (issuer URL), `sub` (subject — the stable user identifier at the provider), `aud` (audience — the client ID of the relying party), `exp` (expiry), `iat` (issued-at), `nonce` (the value the client sent in the authorize request, to defeat replay), `email`, `email_verified`, `name`, `picture`, and others. Because it is a JWT, the client can verify the signature offline using the provider's JWKS public keys, and because the claims are standardized, the client does not need to call a non-standard API to learn who logged in. The client must validate the ID Token exactly like any JWT — check the signature, check `iss` against the expected provider, check `aud` against the client's own ID, check `exp` and `nbf`, check the `nonce` matches what was sent — and only then trust the claims.

OIDC uses the same OAuth 2.0 flows, with the `openid` scope added. The Authorization Code Flow with PKCE is the recommended flow for new applications. The client redirects the user to the provider's `/authorize` endpoint with `scope=openid profile email`, a `nonce` (random string the client generates), and the usual OAuth parameters. After the user authenticates and consents, the provider redirects back with an authorization code. The client exchanges the code at `/token` for three things: an access token (for calling the provider's APIs), an ID Token (the JWT proving who the user is, for the client), and optionally a refresh token. The implicit flow was deprecated because tokens in URLs leak. The hybrid flow returns a signed ID Token in the front channel and the code in the back channel, providing some defense against code substitution; it is rarely used but defined for high-security scenarios.

The `/userinfo` endpoint is the second key piece of OIDC. It is a standardized REST endpoint at the provider that accepts the access token as a Bearer credential and returns the user's claims as JSON. This separation matters because the ID Token is short and focused on identity (the client verifies it once at login), while `/userinfo` is for richer profile data the client may need later (avatar URL, address, custom claims). The two are not redundant: the ID Token is signed and verifiable offline, while `/userinfo` requires an online call but can return more data and is always current. In practice, most consumer apps read the ID Token at login for `sub`, `email`, and `email_verified`, and call `/userinfo` only if they need additional claims. Both the ID Token and the `/userinfo` response must be protected against token substitution attacks: the `nonce` claim in the ID Token binds it to the specific client session, and the `sub` claim in `/userinfo` must match the `sub` in the ID Token.

The discovery document (RFC 8414 / OIDC Discovery 1.0) is what makes OIDC plug-and-play. Every compliant provider publishes a JSON document at `https://provider.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` listing the issuer URL, the authorization endpoint, the token endpoint, the userinfo endpoint, the JWKS URI, the supported scopes, the supported flows, and the supported signing algorithms. A client can be configured with just the issuer URL and discover everything else dynamically. This is why adding a new OIDC provider to a library like NextAuth, Passport, or Spring Security is usually a one-line configuration — the library fetches the discovery document, picks up the JWKS URI, and starts verifying ID Tokens immediately. Microsoft, Google, Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, Keycloak, and Ping Identity all publish discovery documents; an OIDC provider without one is considered broken.

OIDC's relationship to enterprise SSO (SAML) deserves a note. SAML 2.0 (2005) solved enterprise single sign-on before OIDC existed and is still dominant in large enterprises and B2B contexts — Okta, Azure AD, and Ping Identity all support SAML alongside OIDC. SAML uses XML, signed assertions, browser redirects via POST, and is notoriously painful to implement. OIDC is simpler (JSON, JWTs, REST), works natively in browsers and mobile apps, and is the default for new development. The migration is gradual: most enterprise IdPs now support both, with OIDC used for new apps and SAML retained for legacy. The OIDC federation spec (RFC 8485) extends OIDC to support the multi-organization trust relationships that SAML handled natively. The trade-off across both is the same: centralized identity reduces password sprawl but creates a high-value target — the Okta breach of October 2023 affected thousands of federated enterprises.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant RP as Relying Party (Client) participant OP as OpenID Provider participant JWKS as JWKS Endpoint participant UI as /userinfo U->>RP: Click "Log in with Google" RP->>RP: Generate nonce, state, PKCE verifier RP->>U: Redirect to OP /authorize?
scope=openid email profile,
nonce, state, code_challenge U->>OP: Browser follows redirect OP->>U: Show login + consent screen U->>OP: Authenticate + approve OP->>U: Redirect to RP redirect_uri
?code=AUTH_CODE&state=... U->>RP: Browser arrives at RP with code RP->>OP: POST /token (code, code_verifier, client_id) OP->>OP: Verify code, PKCE, client OP-->>RP: id_token (JWT) + access_token + refresh_token RP->>JWKS: GET /.well-known/jwks.json (cached) JWKS-->>RP: public keys RP->>RP: Verify id_token signature,
check iss, aud, exp, nonce RP->>UI: GET /userinfo (Bearer access_token) UI-->>RP: {sub, email, name, picture} RP-->>U: Logged-in session established ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +------+ click login +----------+ | User | --------------> | Relying | +------+ | Party | ^ | (app) | | 1. redirect +----+-----+ | /authorize? | | scope=openid | 2. user authenticates | nonce=N | at OpenID Provider v v +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | OpenID Provider |<--| login + consent | | (Google/Azure AD) | +-------------------+ +---------+---------+ | 3. redirect back with code v +---------+---------+ | Relying Party | | 4. POST /token | | code+verifier | +---------+---------+ | | 5. id_token (JWT) + access_token v +-----------------------------+ | Relying Party verifies: | | - signature via JWKS | | - iss == expected OP | | - aud == own client_id | | - exp in future | | - nonce == N (replay def) | +-------------+---------------+ | | 6. GET /userinfo (Bearer) v +-----------------------------+ | {sub, email, name, picture} | +-----------------------------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The user clicks "Log in with Google" on the relying party (RP); the RP generates a `nonce`, `state`, and PKCE verifier, then redirects the user's browser to the OpenID Provider's `/authorize` endpoint with `scope=openid email profile`, the `nonce`, the `state`, and the PKCE `code_challenge`. 2. The user authenticates at the OpenID Provider (Google, Azure AD, etc.) and approves the consent screen; the provider stores the `nonce` and the user's identity alongside the authorization code it is about to issue. 3. The provider redirects the browser back to the RP's `redirect_uri` with the authorization code and the original `state`; the RP verifies `state` to defeat CSRF. 4. The RP POSTs the code plus the PKCE verifier to the provider's `/token` endpoint and receives three artifacts: an ID Token (JWT), an access token, and optionally a refresh token. 5. The RP fetches the provider's JWKS public keys (cached), verifies the ID Token's signature, and validates `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and the `nonce` (must match what the RP sent) — only then does it trust the ID Token's claims. 6. If the RP needs more profile data than the ID Token carries, it calls the provider's `/userinfo` endpoint with the access token as a Bearer credential and receives the user's claims as JSON; it confirms the `sub` claim matches the ID Token to prevent substitution.

options: First, sign ID Tokens with RS256 or ES256, never HS256 — asymmetric keys let clients verify with the public key without holding the signing secret.

quiz.question: What claims must a client validate in an OIDC ID Token, and what goes wrong if it skips them?
options: Use the authorization code flow with PKCE.
Without nonce validation, the ID Token is vulnerable to replay attacks.
Three options, in increasing order of complexity. First, recommend that the customer use an IdP that supports both SAML and OIDC — Okta, Azure AD, and Ping Identity all do.

quiz.explanation: The client must validate: (1) the JWT signature using the provider's JWKS public keys, pinned to the expected algorithm; (2) iss matches the expected provider URL; (3) aud matches the client's own client ID; (4) exp is in the future; (5) nbf is in the past; (6) nonce matches the value the client sent in /authorize. Skipping the signature check lets an attacker forge any ID Token.
